opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I do a huge amount of my writing by voice now. I'll just go for a walk, or pace around my room, and ramble into my phone. And the thing about how I talk when I'm thinking out loud is that it's a total mess. I'll start a sentence, abandon it halfway, circle back three minutes later to a point I half-made earlier, say "no wait, scratch that," contradict myself, go off on tangents. And the transcription software adds its own layer of chaos on top: it mishears technical terms, so "sparse autoencoder" becomes something bizarre, names get mangled, punctuation is basically random.

Historically, that output was close to useless. Cleaning up a raw dictation transcript by hand takes longer than just writing the thing properly in the first place. So voice was good for brainstorming, but not for producing anything.

What changed is that LLMs are remarkably good at exactly this task. You hand one a wall of garbled, rambling text and say, "This is a dictated brain dump. Fix the transcription errors, figure out what I actually meant, drop the bits where I corrected myself, and organize it into a coherent structure." It does a great job. It can infer from context that the weird phrase was obviously meant to be a technical term. It understands that when I said "actually no," the earlier claim should go. It can notice that the point I made at minute twelve belongs with the one from minute two.

That's a task that's easy for a model and tedious for a human, and it's low stakes: I'm going to read the output anyway, and I know what I meant, so I can catch mistakes immediately. So it's a really good fit for where these systems are reliable.

The bigger benefit for me is that it changes how I think and write. Writing is often bottlenecked on the activation energy of sitting down at a blank page, and on the perfectionism of trying to get each sentence right as you go. Talking separates those things. I can get all my thoughts out at the speed of speech, in whatever order they come, without worrying about quality, and then have the model do the first pass of turning it into prose. Then I edit. Editing a decent draft is so much easier than generating one from nothing. It's probably made me several times more productive at things like writing up research ideas, giving feedback to mentees, or drafting posts.

And there's a practical side too. I can do it while walking, which is nicer than being hunched over a laptop, and I think I often think better when I'm moving. So it's turned dead time into some of my most productive thinking time.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs do a great job turning garbled, rambling dictation into coherent text and describes the task as easy for a model but tedious for a human.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly one of the biggest productivity wins I've had in the last couple of years, and it's kind of mundane, which I think is part of why people underrate it.

So the basic thing is: I think much faster than I type. Most people do. And if I'm trying to write up a research idea, or give feedback on a draft, or explain something to a collaborator, the bottleneck is often not having the thought, it's the friction of getting it out of my head and into text. Typing is slow, and worse, it makes me self-edit as I go, which means I'm trying to do two things at once, generate the idea and polish it, and I end up doing both badly.

So what I do now is just... talk. I'll dictate for five or ten minutes, totally stream of consciousness, and the transcript is a mess. There are false starts, I'll say "wait, no, scratch that," I'll repeat myself three times with slightly different phrasings because I'm figuring out what I mean as I say it, there'll be transcription errors where the model heard "sparse autoencoder" as something bizarre. If you showed that raw transcript to someone it would be close to useless.

And this is exactly the thing LLMs are weirdly good at. You hand it this mess and say, "turn this into a clean document, keep my voice, don't add anything I didn't say," and it just does it. It figures out which of my three phrasings was the one I settled on, it drops the "um, actually, let me back up," it fixes the obvious transcription errors from context. The output is maybe eighty percent of what I'd have written if I'd carefully typed it out, but it took a fifth of the time and, crucially, a tiny fraction of the willpower.

I think the willpower point is actually the important one. There's a lot of stuff I just wouldn't have written otherwise. Like, a long thoughtful comment on someone's doc, or a writeup of a half-baked idea so a mentee can push on it. The activation energy to sit down and type that was too high, so it didn't happen. Now the activation energy is "talk at my phone while walking," and that's low enough that it does happen.

The other thing I'll flag is that this is a fairly safe use of the models, in the sense that they're not being asked to have good ideas or be correct about anything. They're being asked to reorganise text that I produced. The failure modes are things like it slightly smoothing over a nuance I cared about, and I can catch that on a read-through. It's not like asking a model to do my research for me, where the failure mode is a plausible-sounding wrong answer. It's basically a very good editor that has no opinions, and that turns out to be exactly what I want for this task.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs are good at cleaning up messy dictation, but does not state that they handle it better than humans.

astra-6.text:
I find that speaking is a much lower-friction way of getting thoughts out of my head than typing, but what comes out is often a mess. I’ll repeat myself, go off on a tangent, or realise halfway through a sentence that I want to say something different. And transcription errors add another layer of mess.

LLMs are useful because they can often infer what I meant from the context. I can give one this rambling transcript and ask it to turn it into coherent prose while preserving the substance and my tone. That lets me separate getting the ideas out from making them readable.

You do have to check the result, because making something sound polished isn’t the same as faithfully capturing what you meant. But editing a reasonably good draft is often much easier than starting from a blank page.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs can infer intent from rambling transcripts and produce coherent prose, but it does not say they handle messy dictation better than humans.

sol-6.1.text:
When I dictate something, I tend to ramble. I’ll repeat myself, change my mind halfway through a sentence, and get the ideas down in whatever order they occur to me. That’s quite a useful way to think, but it doesn’t produce something you’d want to send to another person.

An LLM can take that mess and turn it into reasonably clear prose. You can say, “Here’s a transcript. Clean it up, preserve what I’m actually saying, and don’t add things.” It’s good at recovering the intended meaning even when the transcription has mistakes or the sentences don’t quite make sense.

So it separates getting the ideas out of my head from making them readable. I can talk without constantly editing myself, and then have something coherent to work from.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs can turn messy dictation into clear prose, but it does not state that they handle it better than humans.
